narration.text: Before snowy travel, clear the windows, hood, trunk and roof so snow does not block your view or the following driver's windshield. Use low beams in snowy conditions even in daylight to make the vehicle visible. If a squall is approaching or known to be nearby, leave the roadway and wait for it to pass. When a highway traffic pack removes the space cushion, slowing by two or three mph can help surrounding traffic clear away. Clear snow, ice and dirt from headlights, taillights and direction indicators. Before snowy driving, let the engine warm so the defroster can warm the windshield and melt remaining ice.

why_how.text: Large trucks, farm equipment and horse-drawn vehicles may accelerate slowly when joining traffic.
On long or steep climbs, trucks typically use flashers to warn they are moving slowly.
An orange rear triangle identifies farm or horse-drawn vehicles designed for speeds of twenty-five miles per hour or less.
Stay well behind tractors and horse-drawn vehicles and do not sound the horn to pass.
Brake lights signal slowing or stopping; if other drivers may not expect braking, quickly tap the pedal three or four times.
When required to travel below forty miles per hour on a limited-access highway, use hazard flashers to warn following drivers.
A turn signal communicates the intended turn but does not give the driver priority to make it.
When driving below thirty-five miles per hour, signal at least one hundred feet before turning.
When driving at thirty-five miles per hour or faster, signal at least three hundred feet before turning.
Use hand signals if the vehicle's turn indicators fail.
A left-turn hand signal extends the left arm horizontally out from the vehicle.
A right-turn hand signal bends the left arm upward at the elbow.
The hand signal for slowing or stopping directs the left arm downward.
For a highway breakdown, signal and pull off carefully, park well clear where others can see, switch on hazards and raise the hood.
Use the horn when a pedestrian or driver may not see you or a vehicle appears about to strike you.
If vehicle control is lost, sound the horn to warn other drivers.
When passing a cyclist after oncoming traffic has cleared, leave at least four feet of passing space.
